data.name: Slovenia
data.summary: Slovenia taxes capital gains and dividends at 25%. The capital gains rate falls to 20% after 5 years, 15% after 10 and 0% after 15 years of holding. Children are fully exempt from inheritance and gift tax, and there is no wealth tax. No special regime for wealthy arrivals.

regimes.name: Ordinary tax residence
regimes.description: Worldwide taxation of residents; capital income taxed separately at schedular rates as a final tax.
regimes.eligibility: Tax resident under the permanent residence, habitual abode, centre of vital interests or 183-day tests.

capital_gains.summary: Capital gains on shares, bonds, fund units and real estate are taxed at a flat 25% final tax (Art. 132 ZDoh-2), reduced by holding period: 20% after 5 years, 15% after 10 years, and exempt after 15 years. Applies to domestic and foreign assets alike.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: Exempt after 15 years of holding (20 years until 31 Dec 2021). Main home exempt if owned, registered as permanent residence and actually lived in for the last 3 years. Gains inside an individual investment account (INR, from 5 Mar 2026) are taxed only on withdrawal at 15%, and the first withdrawal after 15 years is exempt; contributions are capped (EUR 20,000 in year one, then EUR 5,000/yr plus EUR 5,000 for Slovenian instruments, EUR 150,000 lifetime), so INR is immaterial for a large portfolio.
capital_gains.eligibility_conditions: Holding period counted per lot under FIFO (Art. 103 ZDoh-2). Losses offset only capital gains of the same year; a 30-day wash-sale rule disallows losses where identical securities are bought 30 days before or after.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: A gift of capital is a disposal for the donor, but for gifts to a spouse or child the gain can be deferred to the recipient's later sale (application within 15 days). Inheritance is not a disposal. Derivatives are taxed under a separate tax on gains from derivative instruments.

open_questions: No deemed-disposal exit tax for individuals is described in the FURS 2026 capital income guide; not checked against the full ZDoh-2 text.
capital_gains.rate_basis: Rates shown assume holding beyond 15 years (0%). Shorter holdings: 25% (0–5 years), 20% (5–10), 15% (10–15). An actively rebalanced portfolio will realise most gains at 25%.
capital_gains.professional_trader: If securities trading is carried on as a business activity, the income becomes business income under the progressive scale (top bracket 45% or 50% depending on the year, per the FURS guide; not verified for 2026) instead of capital gains; private investing is normally treated as capital gains.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: 25% → 20% after 5 years → 15% after 10 years → 0% after 15 years; FIFO per identical security.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Residents are taxed on worldwide gains; foreign tax paid can be credited. Must self-report gains on foreign brokers (annual return by 28 Feb).

dividends.summary: Dividends are taxed at a flat 25% final tax (Art. 132 ZDoh-2), with no holding-period reduction. Foreign dividends are taxed at 25% with a credit for foreign withholding tax.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: EUR 1,000 annual exemption applies only to interest on bank deposits with Slovenian/EU banks, not to dividends. INR account dividends are taxed only on withdrawal (15%).

inheritance.summary: Inheritance and gift tax (ZDDD) is levied on the recipient, but children, adopted children and their descendants, spouse and unmarried partner (first inheritance order) are fully exempt, for both inheritances and gifts.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: First-order exemption (Art. 9 ZDDD) also covers sons/daughters-in-law and stepchildren. Other heirs: movables-only transfers below EUR 5,000 exempt.
inheritance.important_exceptions: Rates for non-exempt recipients (Art. 8): 5%–14% (parents, siblings), 8%–17% (grandparents), 12%–39% (others). A lifetime gift of shares or real estate is a capital-gains disposal for the parent unless deferral to the child is claimed (see capital gains).

inheritance.gift_tax: Same tax as inheritance; gifts to children are exempt. Gifts must be declared within 15 days.
inheritance.foreign_assets: Applies to property received by Slovenian residents, including foreign assets; children exempt regardless.
inheritance.domicile_rules: Liability attaches to the recipient's residence or the location of Slovenian property; no tail rules found.

income.name: Slovenia

income_tax.summary: Progressive income tax of 16% to EUR 9,721.43, 26% to 28,592.44, 33% to 57,184.88, 39% to 82,346.23 and 50% above, after a general allowance of EUR 5,551.93 (higher at low incomes). Employees pay 22.1% social security plus 1% long-term care; the self-employed bear the employee and employer shares.
income_tax.self_employed_notes: PwC (other taxes) lists employee rates 22.10% (pension 15.50, health 6.36, unemployment 0.14, parental 0.10) and employer rates 16.10% (pension 8.85, health 6.56, unemployment 0.06, injury 0.53, parental 0.10), plus long-term care of 1% for employees, 1% for employers and, expressly, 2% of the relevant base for the self-employed. A compulsory supplementary health contribution of EUR 39.36 a month applies March 2026 to February 2027. The recorded self-employed rate 40.2% = 22.1% + 16.1% + 2% is DERIVED: it assumes sole proprietors bear both the employee and employer shares (Remote Work Europe says they 'bear both shares'); PwC does not list self-employed rates, and the injury share may not apply. The contribution base (minimum/maximum) and any ceiling were not found, so no cap is recorded. Flat-rate (normirani) expense rules for sole proprietors were not found. Employee social_security_deductible: BDO guide is from 2022 (22.1% rate); the recorded 23.1% includes the 1% long-term-care contribution added later, assumed deducted alike. Medium confidence.
income_tax.local_tax_note: No municipal income tax. The general allowance is EUR 5,551.93 for income at or above EUR 17,766.18 and is larger below that; the recorded value is the flat amount.

regimes.name: Digital nomad permit
regimes.description: Temporary residence permit for non-EU nationals employed by, or under a civil-law contract with, a business based outside Slovenia, or self-employed abroad, working entirely remotely with ICT (gov.si, 21 Nov 2025). Requires monthly funds of at least twice the average monthly net salary in Slovenia (figure from the Official Gazette; any lawful income counts). Valid up to one year and 'cannot be extended'; a new application is possible six months after expiry, or a different permit type (e.g. employment) during validity. Family may join immediately. No flat tax for foreign remote workers: a resident pays the normal scale. The euro threshold (about EUR 3,200 net a month on Remote Work Europe, EUR 38,400 a year; a teaser there says about EUR 3,098) could not be tied to the Official Gazette figure.
regimes.duration_note: Up to one year, cannot be extended; re-application possible six months after expiry (gov.si).

sources.title: Slovenia digital nomad permit guide (Remote Work Europe)

open_questions: The monthly amount (2x average net wage, Official Gazette) was not found on an official page; EUR 3,200 net is from Remote Work Europe, which also quotes EUR 3,098. The test is on net funds, so the gross equivalent is higher (not derived here).
Permit is one year and non-renewable (gov.si), so a two-year stay requires a six-month gap or another permit type.
Whether permit holders become tax residents (183 days) was not covered by the opened pages.

regimes.name: Special tax base for seconded employees
regimes.description: For employees seconded to or from abroad for more than 30 uninterrupted days, with a workplace over 200 km away, a salary of at least 1.5 times the last known Slovenian average wage and no tax residence in the secondment country in the previous five years, 20% of salary (capped at EUR 1,000 a month) is excluded from the tax base. Covers income paid within at most 60 months in a 10-year period.
regimes.duration_note: Maximum 60 months within 10 years from the first secondment.

succession.name: Slovenia
succession.summary: Descendants, the spouse and partners are guaranteed half of their intestate share, other close relatives a third. A foreign resident can choose the law of their nationality (EU Succession Regulation art. 22). Slovenia has no trusts; foundation law was not confirmed for private use.
succession.reserved_share: Necessary heirs: descendants, adopted children, parents, spouse and partners; grandparents and siblings only if permanently unable to work and without means (Inheritance Act, ZD, art. 25). Share per art. 26: descendants and spouse one half of the intestate share, others one third (figures from the statute as known, not stated on e-Justice).
succession.foreign_law_note: EU Succession Regulation: the law of the last habitual residence applies by default (art. 21), but a resident foreign national may choose the law of their nationality (art. 22).
succession.trust_note: Slovenia is not in the HCCH table for the 1985 Trusts Convention. Slovenian law has no trust. Foundations (ustanove) are governed by the Institutes Act; their private-benefit use was not researched.
open_questions: The 1/2 and 1/3 shares (ZD art. 26) were not confirmed from a source and should be verified.
The foundation statute (Zakon o ustanovah) and whether private-benefit foundations are possible were not sourced.
Special rules for permanently incapable descendants not captured.
